articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Shadow Fleet Networks, Issues New General Licenses, and Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations targeting individuals, companies, and vessels involved in Iranian shadow fleet networks. This action is part of Washington's ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign, which aims to restrict Iranian financial and commercial networks supporting Tehran's military activities, missile development, cyber operations, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Specifically, OFAC designated five individuals, four companies, and nine vessels, including a Panama-based law firm, Karnakis and Karnakis, and shipping businesses linked to Singapore and the United Arab Emirates. The designated companies also include Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading, Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore, and UAE-based Whales Shipping Line.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued Iran General License GG, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Karnakis and Karnakis, and Iran General License HH, authorizing wind-down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain persons or vessels blocked on October 21, 2026. Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities. OFAC also removed certain Belarus and North Korea designations and issued two amended Frequently Asked Questions, FAQ 1224 and FAQ 1225.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities for Intellectual Property Theft, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has implemented new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA), targeting Chinese entities involved in trade-secret theft and related support. This action aims to protect American intellectual property from foreign adversaries.

OFAC added Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co Ltd, Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management Co Ltd (MiraclePlus), and three affiliated Beijing entities to its Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List. These designations impose blocking and additional lending, foreign-exchange, banking, and investment restrictions on the listed entities.

To accompany these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026, through January 19, 2027.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License for Earthquake Relief Efforts
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 60A, titled 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela.' This amendment aims to facilitate humanitarian aid and recovery efforts in the country.

In addition to the amended general license, OFAC also issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, to provide further clarity and guidance on authorized transactions related to earthquake relief.
This action underscores OFAC's commitment to ensuring that sanctions do not impede legitimate humanitarian activities, particularly in times of crisis.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Financial Networks and Cuban State-Owned Bank, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, targeting financial networks and a state-owned bank. These actions are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' a campaign to disrupt Iran's financial and petroleum sectors and its ability to circumvent sanctions.

OFAC designated several financial institutions, companies, exchange houses, and individuals pursuant to Executive Order 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy. Among the principal targets is the Iraq-based International Development Bank for Investment and Finance (IDB), accused of providing financial facilitation services and U.S. dollar access for Iran.

In a coordinated action, the U.S. Department of State also designated Cuba-based Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA), which is alleged to have provided services to the sanctioned Iran-based Karafarin Bank since at least 2022. OFAC also issued new and amended General Licenses, including Iran-related General License FF, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, and Russia-related General Licenses 128D and 130B.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez Gómez from Sanctions List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has removed Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez, the president of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List). This action lifts restrictions on a prominent political figure and signals a strategic shift in Washington's sanctions policy toward Venezuela.

The removal covers Rodríguez and the alternative names associated with his designation under the Venezuela sanctions program, with all five entries sharing the same identifying information. This means Rodríguez is no longer subject to asset-blocking restrictions, allowing U.S. persons to engage in previously prohibited transactions with him, provided no other sanctions apply.

While OFAC did not publicly explain the reason for the removal, it comes amid continued scrutiny of U.S. economic restrictions on Venezuela and follows earlier delistings of other Venezuelan officials and entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorism financing networks, aiming to disrupt their operations and financial support.
These designations are part of ongoing efforts by the U.S. government to combat global illicit activities that pose threats to national security and international stability.

The specific details of the designated individuals and entities, including their locations and alleged roles in these illicit networks, have been added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List).

articles.headline: OFAC Designates International Criminal Court, Issues General Licenses, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated the entire International Criminal Court (ICC) to its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) pursuant to Executive Order 14203. This unprecedented action targets the institution itself, expanding beyond previous sanctions that primarily focused on individual ICC officials.

In conjunction with the designation, OFAC issued four general licenses: GL 13, authorizing a 180-day wind-down period for certain transactions involving the ICC; GL 14, authorizing transactions related to telecommunications and enterprise software; GL 15, authorizing transactions related to pension payments; and GL 16, authorizing transactions related to certain ICC detainees.

This move has been met with strong reactions, with the EU expressing regret and urging the U.S. to reverse the measures, while the UN Secretary-General condemned the decision. OFAC stated the action was taken to defend U.S. sovereignty and neutralize the threat posed by the ICC. Additionally, OFAC announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics and a Burma-related designation removal.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Russia-Related General License Authorizing Importation of Russian Diesel Fuel
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Russia-related General License 135, authorizing certain transactions related to the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel. This temporary authorization is valid through April 7, 2027.
This action comes amidst rising global diesel prices and follows an announcement by the U.S. President regarding a deal with Russia to release significant amounts of diesel fuel to global markets.

While the general license aims to provide relief to global energy markets, it does not authorize debits to accounts on the books of a U.S. financial institution of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, the National Wealth Fund of the Russian Federation, or the Ministry of Finance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New General License, and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities and financial networks supporting the Iranian regime.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License to facilitate certain authorized transactions. The specifics of this general license aim to provide clarity for legitimate activities while maintaining pressure on sanctioned entities.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License. This amendment adjusts existing authorizations concerning Russia, reflecting the dynamic nature of sanctions policy in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs. These programs include those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, with a total transaction value of approximately $14.83 million. The failures were attributed to deficiencies in payment screening, delayed sanctions watchlist updates, weaknesses in alert prioritization, and human errors involving accounts associated with blocked individuals.

OFAC determined that the violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement amount reflects no reduction to the base penalty, including no mitigation for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarding firm, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC's Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

Between September 2023 and February 2024, Pegasus dealt in blocked property by facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company. The company also failed to respond fully to an OFAC subpoena for six months.

OFAC determined that Pegasus's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed. The settlement amount reflects consideration of general factors under OFAC's Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1.4 Million
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs. The details of the violations and the specific sanctions program were not immediately disclosed in the summary.
This settlement underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts against individuals who violate U.S. sanctions laws, regardless of their affiliation with larger entities.
The penalty amount reflects OFAC's assessment of the severity of the violations and other factors outlined in its enforcement guidelines.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 for Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs. The specific nature of the violations was not detailed in the summary.
This enforcement action highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for all companies, regardless of size, to ensure adherence to U.S. sanctions regulations.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's consideration of various factors, including the company's cooperation and remedial actions taken.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Signals Continued Vigilance on Inflation Amidst Mixed Economic Data
body: The Federal Reserve continues to signal a cautious approach to monetary policy, emphasizing its commitment to bringing inflation back to its 2% target. Recent statements from Fed officials indicate that while some progress has been made, inflationary pressures persist in certain sectors of the economy.

Analysts are closely watching upcoming economic indicators, including the latest consumer price index (CPI) and producer price index (PPI) reports, for further clues on the trajectory of inflation and the potential for future interest rate adjustments. The labor market remains a key focus, with strong employment figures potentially contributing to wage-driven inflation.

Market reactions have been mixed, with investors weighing the prospects of a soft landing against the risk of a prolonged period of higher interest rates. The Fed's next policy meeting is anticipated to provide more detailed guidance on its forward-looking strategy.

articles.headline: Global Oil Prices Fluctuate Amidst Geopolitical Tensions and Supply Concerns
body: Global oil prices experienced significant fluctuations this week, driven by ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and persistent concerns about crude oil supply. Brent crude futures saw an initial surge before paring some gains as market participants assessed the latest developments.

Analysts point to the conflict in the Red Sea region and its potential impact on shipping routes as a primary factor contributing to market volatility. Any disruption to major oil transit chokepoints could lead to further price increases.

Demand-side concerns, particularly from major economies, are also playing a role. While some forecasts suggest a robust demand outlook, others highlight potential headwinds from slower global economic growth, creating a complex environment for oil markets.

articles.headline: EU and UK Trade Negotiations Face New Hurdles Over Regulatory Alignment
body: Trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are encountering fresh obstacles, primarily centered on issues of regulatory alignment. Both sides are struggling to find common ground on standards for goods and services, impacting various sectors.

The latest round of talks concluded with limited progress, and officials from both blocs acknowledged the complexity of bridging existing divergences. The agricultural sector and digital services are among the areas where significant disagreements persist.

Businesses on both sides of the English Channel are closely monitoring the negotiations, with many expressing concerns about potential disruptions to supply chains and increased administrative burdens if a comprehensive agreement remains elusive.

articles.headline: Humanitarian Crisis Deepens in Gaza Amidst Ongoing Conflict
body: The humanitarian crisis in the Gaza Strip has deepened significantly, with international aid organizations warning of catastrophic conditions for civilians. Reports indicate severe shortages of food, water, medicine, and fuel, exacerbated by ongoing hostilities and restrictions on aid delivery.

Hospitals are struggling to cope with the influx of casualties and a critical lack of supplies, leading to widespread concerns about the collapse of the healthcare system. Displaced populations are facing dire circumstances in overcrowded shelters with inadequate sanitation.

International calls for a sustained ceasefire and unimpeded humanitarian access continue to mount, but efforts to de-escalate the conflict and ensure the safe passage of aid have so far yielded limited results.

articles.headline: Political Instability and Security Challenges Persist Across the Sahel Region
body: The Sahel region continues to grapple with widespread political instability and escalating security challenges, marked by a series of coups and the persistent threat of extremist groups. Several nations in the region are experiencing heightened tensions and internal conflicts.

Humanitarian organizations are reporting a growing number of internally displaced persons and refugees as a result of the violence, further straining already limited resources. Food insecurity remains a significant concern across the Sahel.

International efforts to stabilize the region and address the root causes of instability, including poverty and climate change, are ongoing but face considerable hurdles amidst the complex political and security landscape.

articles.headline: Continued Violence and Human Rights Concerns in Myanmar
body: Myanmar continues to be plagued by widespread violence and severe human rights abuses, with reports of ongoing clashes between military forces and armed resistance groups. The humanitarian situation remains critical for many civilians.

International observers and human rights organizations have condemned the escalating violence and called for an end to the repression of dissent. Access for independent monitors and aid agencies remains severely restricted in many areas.
The international community is exploring various diplomatic avenues to address the crisis, but a clear path towards a peaceful resolution and the restoration of democratic governance remains elusive.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties Against American Express and Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its enforcement actions for October 2026, including significant civil money penalties against American Express National Bank and Bank of America, National Association.

American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, received a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations.

Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for similar deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties for embezzlement.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
